wa_exit_38.blurb: Exit 38 is a cluster of small cliffs scattered through the hills beside the interstate near North Bend, east of Seattle. Three main sections hold most of the climbing: Mt Washington, nearest the ramp, Deception Crags, a short way down the road, and Far Side, the farthest out and the biggest by route count. Sport climbing dominates, mostly 5.10 to 5.12, with a fair spread of moderates from 5.6 to 5.9, plus well over a hundred boulder problems and some mixed and drytooling lines. Trad is uncommon. The stone is metamorphic, hard but fractured and brittle in places, and many routes climb better than they look, on steep juggy faces with a few slabs. Deception offers sun or shade at nearly any hour, while most Far Side crags face south. Dry climbing runs roughly April into mid-October; rain makes November through March unreliable.

ca_running_springs_area.blurb: Running Springs sits high in the San Bernardino Mountains, around 6,000 feet, with its biggest concentration of climbing on Keller Peak. Farther east, around Green Valley Lake at better than 7,000 feet, short trad formations and boulders are strewn across the hillsides, and Snow Valley adds a large field of boulder problems. The climbing splits almost evenly between bouldering and trad, with a smaller share of sport and top-rope. Most roped lines fall between 5.7 and 5.10, with some harder sport climbs up to 5.12, and boulder problems lean toward the easy and moderate end. Across this range most climbing is on granite, and it is mostly single-pitch and short: variety of style and setting rather than height is the draw.

ca_volcanic_tablelands_happy_sad_boulder.blurb: A volcanic plateau just north of Bishop, where the Owens Valley floor lifts abruptly into a mesa cut by canyons and washes. Happy Boulders and Sad Boulders are the two main drainages, close together and similar in style, with the Happys the larger. Nearly everything here is bouldering, with problems from V0 to V12: a broad supply of easy and moderate lines and a thinner tail of hard ones. The rock is hard volcanic tuff from the Bishop Tuff, in generally shorter boulders sheltered inside the canyons, with gymnastic movement, thoughtful traverses and some achievable highballs. On stormy winter days the canyons give more wind shelter than the Buttermilks, and Bishop as a whole climbs best from October through March.

ny_the_trapps.blurb: The Trapps is the longest and most popular cliff of the Gunks, near New Paltz, a few miles long and ranging from about 30 to over 250 feet high. Climbs are one to three pitches, mostly trad on quartz conglomerate, whose horizontal cracks, roofs and jugs define the style. Grades run from easy fives up to 5.13, with the bulk between 5.8 and 5.11, and a large collection of boulder problems sits beneath the cliff. The face is divided into named sections such as the Uberfall, the Arrow Wall and the Yellow Wall, so you can pick an easy or hard stretch to suit the day. Fall, especially September and October, is the prime season; spring is busy but wetter and buggier, and summer is hot and humid.

va_charlottesville_vicinity.blurb: Climbing around Charlottesville is mostly bouldering, spread across the Blue Ridge Parkway, local parks and a scatter of small spots. The Parkway holds by far the largest share, including one forest area with the biggest concentration of greenstone boulders in the region, where a few hard problems sit among many easier ones. Wintergreen, roughly an hour southwest of the city, is a small granite crag with about fifty climbs, mostly trad plus some top-rope and a few bolted lines. Roped climbs mostly fall between 5.6 and 5.11 and boulder problems run from V0 into the high V-grades. Everything is short single-pitch climbing, a local, low-key scene rather than a big-wall destination.

ut_american_fork_canyon.blurb: A narrow, deep canyon in the Southern Wasatch, with crags on both sides of the road and a river running through tall pines. Sport climbing is the story: steep, pocket-filled limestone, mostly 5.10 to 5.13 with 5.11 and 5.12 the heart of it, and a smaller supply of moderates around 5.8 and 5.9. Some of Utah's hardest routes are in the cave of the Hell Area, while walls such as the Hideaway, Hard Rock and Tank Canyon spread the climbing around. Trees shade belayers through the summer heat. The main season runs from spring through fall; winter brings freezing temperatures. Bouldering is a minor extra, including some granite boulders near Silver Lake.
